title: Application of an upsampling algorithm to quantum state preparation of continuous and discrete probability distributions
abstract_summary: The paper adapts a classical upsampling approach to construct quantum state vectors whose amplitudes are square roots of probabilities sampled from continuous distributions (supported on the real line) and arbitrary discrete distributions. The resulting divide-and-conquer circuit of controlled y-rotations can be transformed via quantum forking into an equivalent polylogarithmic-depth circuit; the method is demonstrated with Gaussian, Laplace and binomial examples and is extensible to other (including multivariate) distributions.
methodology_description: The paper develops a theoretical quantum-state-preparation methodology based on classical upsampling of a probability density function (PDF). For a target univariate continuous PDF P(x) (support on R) the method maps 2^n computational basis amplitudes to equally spaced sample locations xn = x0 + (w/2^n)·in inside a capture window of width w, with an optional small random shift parameter ζ to avoid aliasing. Amplitudes are defined from a periodicized form of the PDF: ξ_n(xn) = sqrt( δ_xn · Σ_j P(xn + j w) ), where δ_xn is a normalization factor. The paper derives a recursive reduction for δ_xn and for the amplitude coefficients using the identity that splits sums over period-shifted samples; this yields closed-form expressions for controlled single-qubit y-rotation angles θ_{n,m}(i) expressed as arccosine ratios of partial sums of the periodicized PDF. The state-preparation circuit is a divide-and-conquer network of controlled Ry gates (controlled by bit patterns of basis indices) that implements those angles (exponential gate depth in the naive construction). For reduction of depth the authors apply a quantum-forking transformation (per Araujo et al.) that introduces one control qubit, O(2^n) ancillas and controlled-swap structures to produce an equivalent circuit with polylogarithmic depth. The method is adapted to discrete probability distributions by constructing a state that embeds probabilities and their complements into the periodic sampling (using Dirac-delta approximations by narrow Gaussians) which simplifies angle formulas: θ_{n,1}(i) = 2 arccos(sqrt(P(i))) and θ_{n,m>1} = π/2. The paper demonstrates the approach on examples (Gaussian, Laplace, lognormal, binomial), shows how to compute the rotation angles from analytic PDFs or discrete probabilities, and reports simulation illustrations of the prepared distributions (e.g., n=3 examples converted to the quantum-forking circuit). No empirical financial dataset or hardware execution is used — the work is algorithmic/theoretical with simulated circuit examples.
algorithms_used: Quantum forking (Araujo et al. depth reduction)

results_summary: The paper develops an upsampling-based quantum state-preparation algorithm that maps sampled values of a continuous probability density P(x) (or a discrete probability vector) into amplitudes of an n-qubit state. The construction forms a periodic extension of the density over a sampling window, derives closed-form expressions for the Ry rotation angles in a divide-and-conquer controlled-rotation circuit, and shows how discrete distributions can be represented via an auxiliary complementary state. Although the native divide-and-conquer circuit has exponential gate depth, the author argues (referencing existing quantum-forking techniques) that it can be converted to an equivalent circuit of polylogarithmic depth at the expense of ancilla qubits (d = 2^n - 1) and extra controlled-swap operations. The paper includes numerical/simulation examples for Gaussian, Laplace, and binomial distributions to illustrate the approach and states the method is extendable to other distributions and to multivariate cases.
performance_claims: Δx_n (sampling interval) = w / 2^n (definition of sampling resolution).
Native divide-and-conquer circuit exhibits exponential gate-depth (no explicit big-O provided for the naive version).
Conversion to quantum-forking form requires one control qubit and d = 2^n - 1 ancilla qubits and a set of d - 1 controlled-swap gates (resource overhead).
After conversion the gate-depth is claimed to be polylogarithmic; the paper references a gate-depth scaling quoted as O(log2 2(d)) in the text (as cited from prior work).

For discrete probability amplitudes the top-level rotation angles simplify to θ = 2 arccos(√P) and for deeper levels (m > 1) rotations reduce to π/2 (Hadamards) in the singular-limit construction shown.
quantum_advantage_detail: The paper does not present an empirical demonstration of end-to-end quantum advantage over classical state-loading methods. It proposes a method that in its native form has exponential circuit depth but claims — by invoking prior quantum-forking results — that the circuit can be transformed to polylogarithmic depth (theoretical complexity improvement) at the cost of substantial ancilla qubits and controlled-swap overhead. This is presented as a theoretical/algorithmic complexity claim rather than an experimentally demonstrated advantage.
limitations: The native upsampling circuit is a divide-and-conquer algorithm with exponential gate depth (author-stated), requiring transformation (quantum forking) to achieve polylogarithmic gate depth.
The approximation ξn(xn) ≈ sqrt(P(xn) δxn) relies on choosing the sampling window w 'sufficiently large' so that the periodic sum over jw reduces to a single term (author-stated).
Use of a random small shift parameter ζ is required to avoid aliasing when resampling the PDF; choice and management of ζ affect the produced amplitudes (author-stated).

key_ideas: #idea:hybrid-approach — Uses classical upsampling of a PDF to compute sample values and closed-form Ry rotation angles, then implements quantum state preparation via a divide-and-conquer controlled-Ry circuit.

#idea:quantum-advantage — Claims that applying a quantum-forking transformation converts the naive exponential-depth prepare circuit into an equivalent polylogarithmic-depth circuit, enabling efficient amplitude loading in principle.

#limitation:qubit-count — The polylogarithmic-depth construction requires a large number of ancilla qubits (d = 2^n - 1) and many controlled-swaps, shifting cost from depth to qubit-count and connectivity.
#limitation:simulation-only — Demonstrations are numerical/simulation illustrations (small n examples, e.g., n=3); no real-hardware runs or empirical financial datasets are provided.

#limitation:data-encoding — The approach relies on windowed periodic sampling, approximations (e.g., narrow Gaussians for delta functions) and a sampling-resolution trade-off (Δx = w / 2^n) that affect approximation error and resource needs.

#idea:hybrid-approach — For discrete distributions the method yields analytic simplifications (top-level rotation θ = 2 arccos(√P) and deeper rotations collapsing to π/2 in the singular-limit construction) and uses an auxiliary complementary state to represent arbitrary discrete vectors.

#idea:quantum-advantage — The author argues the method is extensible to multivariate distributions (via tensor-product sampling) and to other continuous families, suggesting applicability to Monte Carlo workflows in finance.
contradictions: #contradiction:scalability — The paper asserts polylogarithmic gate depth after applying quantum-forking but simultaneously requires exponentially many ancilla qubits (d = 2^n - 1) and O(d) controlled-swaps; this trade-off undermines practical scalability for large n and shifts complexity from depth to qubit resources.

#contradiction:classical-vs-quantum — The manuscript claims broad applicability to financial and scientific applications and implies efficient quantum loading of probability information, but provides no financial-domain examples, benchmarks, or comparisons to classical state-preparation/loading methods, so superiority over classical approaches remains unproven.
